title: Query-optimal quantum simulation of Lindblad evolution
abstract: For the problem of simulating Lindblad evolution for time $t$ to precision $ε$, Hamiltonian simulation provides an additive query lower bound, informally, $Ω(t + \mathrm{polylog}(1/ε))$. However, the best previously known algorithms for general Lindblad simulation achieve a multiplicative upper bound, informally, $\mathcal{O}(t\,\mathrm{polylog}(1/ε))$, in gate complexity. It has remained open whether this multiplicative dependence is necessary. In this paper, we close the gap in query complexity by giving an algorithm with optimal additive dependence on evolution time and precision in the block-encoding model. Our approach uses the transducer framework to reduce the query cost of composing first-order approximations to the evolution channel, together with linear combinations of reuse circuits of different lengths to suppress catalyst-removal error. Although our additional gate complexity is higher than that of existing algorithms, our optimal query complexity resolves the question of how much oracle access is fundamentally necessary and identifies the remaining challenge to achieve the optimal gate complexity.

bite.hook: A new algorithm achieves optimal additive query complexity for simulating Lindblad evolution.
tldr: Addressed the problem of simulating Lindblad evolution for time t to precision epsilon in query complexity.
Used a transducer framework and linear combinations of reuse circuits to suppress catalyst-removal error.
Closed the query complexity gap by providing an algorithm with optimal additive dependence on evolution time and precision.
bite.whyItMatters: Simulating open quantum systems is essential for chemistry and physics, but doing it efficiently requires knowing the absolute mathematical limits of how many times a quantum computer must consult an oracle.
bite.eli5: Imagine trying to predict how a leaky system loses energy to its environment. This research figures out the absolute minimum number of lookups a computer needs to make to get the simulation right.
